prize_parts.citation: for the development of ionizable lipid nanoparticles as carriers for nucleic-acid medicines

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B035 as a single-part prize to Cullis, Hope and Madden. The round-1 exchange did not dispute the science. Every member who addressed it accepted the chemical logic of pKa-tuned ionizable lipids, formulation by controlled assembly and rapid mixing, and endosomal escape through non-bilayer phase propensity and membrane fusion, and no one questioned its maturity or its independent reproduction. It is the one shortlisted achievement where settled clinical proof (approved siRNA drugs, billions of mRNA vaccine doses) coincides with a clear molecular design principle, and it supplies the carrier that the 2023 Medicine prize left unrecognised while honouring the cargo. The objections raised against it are attribution and category, not merit. I address attribution directly: the early work on pH-dependent lipid behaviour, bilayer-to-hexagonal phase propensity and the first controlled-assembly encapsulation of nucleic acids came from the Vancouver group, which is the reason I credit Cullis, Hope and Madden. This is a judgment from the primary literature, not from patent history.
statement.case_against: The credit is the real weakness, and round 1 showed that it is not converging: four members proposed three different sets of names for B035, and the chair counts only two supporters. Anderson's lipidoid route is a genuinely independent line to the same delivery chemistry, MacLachlan and Langer have substantive claims, and any three-person cut excludes people who matter. There is also a fair argument that the achievement is delivery technology with a medical effect rather than a single chemical discovery, and that the 2023 Medicine prize already covered much of the same territory. I weigh these objections seriously. They are strongest if the committee insists on one canonical inventor of the decisive lipid, and weaker if the citation is worded around the design principle and the formulation science.

responses.point: Linke (chair) moved B063 to first place because the credit divides cleanly into a concept strand (Crews, Deshaies) and a mechanism strand (Handa), and says he would regard B035 as a serious rival if the committee could agree on a defensible three, but sees no such agreement yet.
responses.response: I agree that attribution is the deciding issue, and that no agreed trio exists at the moment. My view is that the disagreement is narrower than it looks. Cullis is named in every B035 proposal, and the dispute is whether the other places go to the early assembly and phase-behaviour work or to the lipidoid line. A citation worded around ionizable lipids and their formulation as carriers fits the first reading well, and I would sooner defend that precise scope than a vague one. I also note that B063 is not free of the same problem: you, Aili and Chabes each call the cut contestable, and Ciulli, Ito and Gray are all named as having substantive claims. The difference between the two is that the unsettled part of B035 is who holds the third place, while the unsettled part of B063 includes whether the modality is yet proven in patients.

responses.point: Chabes asks what clinical milestones would justify B063 and argues that its concept and mechanism papers are not contested in priority, unlike the Vancouver-Boston patent history for B035. He weighs the breadth of opening support heavily.
responses.response: The priority point is fair and it is a real advantage for B063, which I said in round 1. I do not accept that patent disputes should count against B035 in a scientific ranking, because the committee reads papers and not claims, and the papers show a clear order of events for ionizable-lipid design and formulation. On breadth of support, I share the chair's caution: all eight members ranked B063, but I ranked it fourth and the three members who prefer it still call it early. Broad inclusion across lists also shows that it is nobody's clear mistake, which is not the same as showing it is the strongest case. On milestones, my own answer to the chair's first question is that a first approval, or a randomised result showing benefit over standard therapy, would remove the main objection and I would then move B063 above B035. Without that, I treat B063 as the next in line, not the lead.

responses.point: Aqvist proposes Cullis with Anderson, argues that the lipidoid route carried lipids into approved products and is free of the Vancouver patent disputes, and asks whether Hope and Madden's lipid-assembly work outweighs the translation route. He also pairs B035 with base editing (B068, Liu alone).
responses.response: This is the question I owe an answer to. I have reconsidered Anderson and I still put the primary weight on the Vancouver work, because the pH-dependent behaviour of ionizable lipids, their phase propensity and their formulation were understood there before the combinatorial screens, and the approved products rest on that chemistry. I accept that this is a judgment, and that Cullis with Anderson is a defensible alternative reading in which the translation route is weighted more heavily. On the second part, I still decline to add base editing. It sits close to the 2020 CRISPR prize, it is under a decade old with long-term safety open, and a two-part prize would make the LNP part a two-name citation that leaves out the early Vancouver contributors I regard as central. A single, well-defined achievement is a stronger public statement than a pairing built to fit three seats.

responses.point: Aili calls B035 the strongest competing case, would be comfortable moving it to first place if the Vancouver allocation is settled, but prefers B063 for conceptual originality, with Handa ahead of Ciulli in a three-person cut.
responses.response: Aili's position is the most useful one for settling this, because it names the single condition under which we would agree. I think the Vancouver allocation can be settled on the primary literature, and I have given my reading above: ionizable-lipid design and formulation science, credited to Cullis, Hope and Madden. On the originality argument for B063, I accept that deliberately inducing proximity to a ubiquitin ligase is a more novel modality than a delivery carrier. My view is that the prize criterion is a discovery or invention of greatest benefit that is mature enough to judge, and on that measure the absence of an approved degrader is a real discount that B035 does not have.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept a Vancouver-centred trio (Cullis, Hope, Madden) or prefer a configuration that includes Anderson's lipidoid route; I regard this as a judgment on the primary literature, not a settled fact.
Whether ionizable lipid nanoparticles will be regarded as chemistry (molecular design and self-assembly) rather than pharmaceutical technology after the 2023 Medicine prize.
Whether a first approved degrader, expected within a few years, would reverse the ordering of B063 and B035; I think it would.
Whether the breadth of B063 support reflects merit or a lack of strong objection, a question the chair has also raised.
statement.conflict_note: No change since round 1. My research on lipid self-assembly, membrane biophysics and amyloid is close to B035 and B046 in subject matter, and I work in Lund Physical Chemistry with colleagues on the committee, but I have no stated tie to any credited candidate. I know of no collaboration or prior association with any credited person and no member has asked me to recuse. I regard the closeness of B035 to my field as a bias to be weighed, not a ground for recusal, and I have tried to test my reading of the Vancouver work against the primary literature and against the objections of Aqvist and Chabes.
